newsitem.title: FRANCE: Arthuis seeks to quash fears on French EMU goals. [CORRECTED 15:36 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Arthuis seeks to quash fears on French EMU goals. [CORRECTED 15:36 GMT]

text.p: Amid persistent talk of French budget worries and a possible snap election, finance minister Jean Arthuis said on Friday (corrects from Thursday) he was confident the country would make the grade this year to join a European single currency.

Arthuis returned from the West African state of Benin to a barrage of media speculation that weaker tax and other revenues could make it harder for the centre-right government to cut the public deficit to the level needed for European monetary union.
"I'm surprised by what I've heard and seen on this matter," Arthuis told reporters at a routine press briefing. "I issued a statement yesterday to ensure there was no misunderstanding."
"As far as the budget is concerned, I say, and I'm repeating it, spending is under control and the government will meet the goal it set itself. We will meet the three-percent goal in 1997."
"I'm not saying here it is an easy job but I am saying there is no reason for worry," he said.

Newspapers have for the last several days cast a parlour of doubt on the state's finances despite predictions of firmer economic growth this year, saying signs of weaker revenues in value added tax (VAT) and weak contributions from wages to the social security system threaten the state finances equation.

Several have splashed stories, saying that internal finance ministry papers paint a "worst scenario" danger of a hefty overshoot on the EMU deficit target and that this could force the government to make further spending cuts at a time of record 12.8 percent unemployment.

As the speculation on both the political and economic fronts fuelled investor nervousness in the financial markets, Arthuis had a statement issued on Wednesday reaffirming that France's public deficit would be cut, as required this year to qualify for a single currency, to the equivalent of three percent of national wealth, or gross domestic product (GDP).

Analysts say one reason Chirac might be tempted to advance elections would be to avoid a campaign for the normal deadline of March 1998 clashing with the crucial period for deciding which countries are allowed into European monetary union. Arthuis refused to be drawn into commenting on the increasingly tense political situation amid mounting press speculation that President Jacques Chirac could dissolve the National Assembly and call early elections to try to secure a renewed centre-right majority for the rest of his seven-year presidential term.

Analysts believe Chirac may seize on a slight brightening of economic prospects -- despite the latest flurry of doubts over the deficit -- and the government's popularity to try to catch the opposition Left unprepared.
Arthuis said figures just released on the first two months of the year had confirmed that the budget deficit was coming down and that March figures should confirm the trend.

He said VAT revenues had probably been hit by the "one-off" impact of recent, faster systems for reimbursing VAT to firms and that the relationship between revenues and reimbursements would even out "in conformity with expectations".
"Moreover, the first indications we have for 1997 (on VAT) are reassuring on this," he said.

Arthuis reiterated his forecasts of minimum 2.3 percent GDP growth this year after just 1.3 percent growth in 1996, and of 2.8 percent economic growth in 1998, when the government will have to find further savings to meet its promise of a an even lower budget deficit -- 2.8 percent of GDP.

France's budget deficit up until the end of February was 72.4 billion francs, 17.6 billion less than at the same stage last year and Arthuis said the signs were that the deficit at end-March to be around 18 billion better than last year.

On the social security deficit, a crucial component of the total public deficit, Arthuis noted that contributions from wages would be helped by growth this year and next which should create 120-140,000 jobs this year and 222-240,000 jobs in 1998.
